en.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones Hunts Killers in AMC+'s "Kill Jackie"
en.summary: AMC+ unleashes "Kill Jackie," a stylish revenge thriller starring Catherine Zeta-Jones as a former drug smuggler forced back into action. Get ready for a high-octane ride as she takes on a deadly squad of assassins.
en.body:
The world of high-stakes thrillers gets a dazzling, if familiar, injection of adrenaline with AMC+'s upcoming series, **Kill Jackie**. Starring the ever-captivating **Catherine Zeta-Jones**, this eight-episode revenge romp plunges viewers into the life of Jackie Price, a woman who has masterfully evaded her past as an international cocaine purveyor for two decades. Living in opulent luxury and dealing in fine art, Jackie has perfected the art of staying in the shadows. However, comfort breeds complacency, and her carefully constructed peace is shattered when the notorious "Seven Demons"—a cartel of the world's most formidable hitmen—are hired to terminate her.

Convinced that a ghost from her clandestine former life is pulling the strings, Jackie decides it's time to trade her elegant art dealings for her equally sharp, albeit deadlier, old instincts. The series transforms into a thrilling game of cat and mouse, or rather, hunter and hunted, with Jackie determined to strike first. The official synopsis hints at unexpected dangers lurking in seemingly mundane places, suggesting that the true threats might not always be the most obvious ones, and that Jackie's own inner demons could prove to be her greatest challenge.

## A Symphony of Stylistic Homages

The creative team behind the acclaimed **Killing Eve** delivers a visually stunning production. From the vibrant, almost hallucinatory cinematography to the impeccably sharp costuming and production design, **Kill Jackie** is a feast for the eyes. The series wears its influences proudly, with the RogerEbert review noting clear nods to the stylistic signatures of **Guy Ritchie**, **Quentin Tarantino**, and the **John Wick** franchise. Elements like snarky voiceovers, a roster of eccentric assassins, and a flair for stylized violence are present, creating a Technicolor vengeance experience that, while undeniably appealing, treads familiar ground. The acting, led by **Zeta-Jones**, is reportedly faultless, elevating the material even as it draws inspiration from its genre predecessors.

## What Fans Can Expect

For fans of the assassin genre, **Kill Jackie** offers a potent cocktail of action, dark humor, and high-stakes drama. The premise of a retired operative forced back into the game is a well-loved trope, and **Catherine Zeta-Jones** is perfectly cast to embody the blend of sophistication and lethal capability required for the role. The series promises a fast-paced narrative filled with stylish set pieces and sharp dialogue, reminiscent of the genre's most celebrated entries. While some critics have pointed out its derivative nature, the show's commitment to its aesthetic and the strength of its lead performance suggest it will be a compelling watch for those who enjoy a well-executed revenge thriller with a distinctive visual flair.

## What's Next

**Kill Jackie** is set to premiere on AMC+ on October 2, 2026, with an eight-episode run. Viewers can anticipate a visually rich and action-packed journey as Jackie Price fights for survival.

content_raw: From the creatives behind “ Killing Eve ,” Catherine Zeta-Jones lands on AMC+ with an assassin show that feels like it was Mad Libs-ed into existence. In “Kill Jackie,” Jackie Price (Zeta-Jones) has spent the past 20 years living in luxury, traveling, and selling fine art in the most complex and eccentric way possible. All while sticking to the shadows. Staying under the radar is essential after escaping her past as a purveyor of the finest cocaine. But when Jackie starts to get too comfortable, life takes a deadly turn: The Seven Demons, a squad of the world’s most fearsome hitmen (apparently), have been hired to kill her. Convinced someone from her past is behind the hit, Jackie revives her old instincts and sets out to return the favor. It’s a get-them-before-they-get-her situation. As the killers close in, Jackie discovers the biggest dangers come from the silliest sources, but the demons within are far more deadly. That will sound lovely to lovers of the genre, but by episode three of this Technicolor vengeance romp (reminiscent of a nose candy bender), it’s clear Guy Ritchie, Quentin Tarantino, and “John Wick” must have teeth marks on them, because they’ve been bitten into. “Kill Jackie” is more derivative than a FUCCI handbag bought on Canal Street in NYC—it looks like the genuine article, but something’s not quite right. The series is certainly visually appealing: the costuming and production design are as snappy as the stunt work. The acting is faultless as well. However, the show borrows so heavily and frequently from its predecessors that it becomes a bombardment of assassin-genre references. Ritchie’s snarky but character-rich voiceovers, John Wick’s cadre of quirky killers, and the “Kill Bill” of it all. You see it when Jackie eventually turns the tables and seeks revenge on the former colleagues who hurt her. She even has a Kill List with the names crossed out. Totally on brand. Everything about this series is a knockoff, down to its seven assassins, The Seven Demons. The first one is meant to be Pedro Pascal. Another is a mashup of Grace Jones and Daryl Hannah as Elle Driver; a third is probably Crispin Glover because he’s bizarrely nerdy and persnickety. Then there’s a retired assassin who looks like a double for Antonio Banderas. Oh, and let’s not forget the potential final boss, an Ian McShane type but younger.   Meanwhile, the show smugly rolls along, leaving very little feeling in the wake of very big eye rolls. For example, lines like “You don’t become Jackie Price without knowing how to win.” Or the Accountant-minion (Daniel Ings) who loudly protests the Wile E. Coyote-style deaths of Jackie’s enemies while handing in receipts from the ACME store (literally). He keeps complaining but remains fully complicit.   However, in moments of clarity, “Kill Jackie” has heart, as we see in Jackie’s relationship with her assistant, Charlie (Hattie Hook).
